title: Kremmling Well Depth and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Kremmling wells have a 163-ft median depth, with finished well costs modeled at $16,600-$28,300.
h1: Kremmling, Colorado Well and Drilling Guide
intro_html:
Buying land around Kremmling means evaluating the well record as carefully as the views, driveway and building site. Permitted wells within 5 miles show a median depth of 163 feet, but the middle half ranges from 60 to 375 feet. Reported yields are generally useful, with a 10.0 gallon-per-minute median among the wells that reported pump yield.

This area is dominated by unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, not Denver Basin groundwater. That makes neighboring well records valuable, but it does not guarantee the same result on your parcel. Use the data to set expectations for depth, production and bidding, then confirm the site with a Colorado driller and the Division of Water Resources permit requirements.

sections.heading: Kremmling well depths vary with the mountain bedrock
sections.html:
The 104 Kremmling-area wells reporting total depth have a 163-foot median. The middle half runs from 60 to 375 feet, so a bid based only on the median can miss the local spread. About 34% of wells are under 100 feet, another 34% fall from 100 to 300 feet, and 28% are from 300 to 600 feet. The 90th percentile is 499 feet, and the deepest recorded well is 1,448 feet.

Permits identify unnamed or fractured-bedrock aquifers for 171 wells, while 3 name Pierre Shale. In granite and gneiss, water commonly depends on fractures rather than a uniform underground layer. A driller should discuss casing, grout and what happens if the first target does not produce.

sections.heading: Most reported Kremmling wells make usable household yields
sections.html:
Only 36 wells report a pump yield, so the production figures are not a guarantee for every parcel. Within that group, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 6.8 to 14.7 gallons per minute. The records show 58% producing from 5 to 15 gallons per minute, 25% at 15 gallons per minute or more, and 17% from 1 to 5 gallons per minute.

No reported well in this set is under 1 gallon per minute. For a buyer, that is encouraging, but a home also needs storage and a properly sized pump. Ask for the neighboring well completion reports, pump tests and any required water-use approval. An exempt household-use well remains subject to its permit conditions and the 35-gallon-per-minute pumping limit.

sections.heading: Kremmling water levels are shallow in the reported records
sections.html:
Only 10 wells report a static water level, so the water-level sample is limited. The median depth to water is 85 feet, with the middle half from 38 to 100 feet. That gives a reasonable local starting point for discussing pump setting and trench work, but it should not be treated as a parcel-specific water table.

The permit totals by decade do not provide a matching water-level series. Because of that, these records do not establish a dropping or rising groundwater trend around Kremmling. Seasonal conditions, well construction and the exact fracture intercepted can affect the measurement. Have the driller check nearby records and measure the proposed well after construction before finalizing pump equipment.

sections.heading: Kremmling permit history points to steady local drilling
sections.html:
The DWR records include 174 permitted wells within 5 miles of Kremmling, with 97 recorded as constructed. Permits were issued in the 1970s, 1980s, 1990s, 2000s, 2010s and 2020s, with the newest permit year being 2025. The largest decade in the record is the 1990s, with 49 permits; the 2000s follow with 38.

Mcpherson Drilling Company, listed with Benny Don Mcpherson, appears most often with 30 records. Aztec Drilling Company, listed with Keith Branstetter, appears with 16, and Authorized, listed with Pe and Pg, appears with 11. These names describe permit history, not a recommendation or proof that a company is available for your project.

sections.heading: A Kremmling well budget starts with fractured-bedrock drilling
sections.html:
The local cost model uses a typical drilling rate of $65 to $100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss. At the 163-foot median depth, the drilled hole models at about $10,600 to $16,300. A finished well with pump, pressure tank, trenching and electrical models at about $16,600 to $28,300.

Those figures are planning ranges, not a fixed bid. Depth is the main variable, and a difficult access route or a deeper-than-expected hole can change the total. Get the drilling rate, casing and grout allowances, testing, pump equipment, electrical work and abandonment terms in writing. Ask what happens financially if the hole is dry or produces less than the household needs.

sections.heading: Check contamination, septic space and dry-hole exposure
sections.html:
The mapped area within about 10 miles includes 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 88 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. These map points do not prove that a particular parcel has contaminated water, but they justify a records review and laboratory testing. Historic mining can also affect site access, soil handling and water-quality questions.

Low yield and dry holes remain practical risks in fractured rock even when nearby wells look good. Before buying, locate the proposed well, septic system, replacement area and house footprint together. Keep required separation distances in the design, confirm the permit path with Colorado DWR and test an existing well for the contaminants relevant to the property. A good yield does not by itself establish safe drinking water.

sections.heading: Use nearby Kremmling records before choosing a lot
sections.html:
Start with wells closest to the parcel, then compare records from Parshall, Heeney, Hot Sulphur Springs, McCoy, Granby and Tabernash when local information is thin. The Kremmling data show both shallow and deep construction, so distance and similar geology matter more than a single countywide average. Pay particular attention to completed wells, reported yields and static levels rather than permit counts alone.

For a build, make the well, septic system, driveway and house layout part of one site review. For a purchase, make the contract and financing decisions contingent on reviewing the permit, construction report, water quality and pump performance. A Colorado driller can estimate the likely depth and equipment, but only the actual hole confirms the water-bearing fractures on your land.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Kremmling, Colorado?
faq.a: The median reported well depth near Kremmling is 163 feet. The middle half ranges from 60 to 375 feet, while the 90th percentile is 499 feet. About 34% are under 100 feet and 28% are from 300 to 600 feet. The deepest recorded well is 1,448 feet, showing how variable fractured mountain bedrock can be.

faq.q: What does a well cost to drill in Kremmling?
faq.a: The local drilling model uses $65 to $100 per foot. At the 163-foot median depth, the drilled hole is modeled at about $10,600 to $16,300. A finished well including pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at about $16,600 to $28,300. Actual cost depends on depth, access, construction and equipment.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Kremmling?
faq.a: Among the 36 Kremmling-area wells reporting pump yield, the median is 10.0 gallons per minute and the middle half is 6.8 to 14.7 gallons per minute. The records show 58% producing from 5 to 15 gallons per minute. Because many wells do not report yield, nearby completed-well records and a pump test are important.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Kremmling?
faq.a: The permit map does not establish drinking-water safety. Within about 10 miles, the records show 4 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 88 historic mine features and 1 EPA Superfund or cleanup site. Test the specific well, review nearby land uses and mining history, and do not assume that a good production rate means the water is safe.

faq.q: Are Kremmling wells getting deeper or drying up?
faq.a: The available records do not establish a groundwater decline. Only 10 wells report static water level, with a median depth to water of 85 feet and a middle half from 38 to 100 feet. The permit-by-decade totals are not a matching water-level trend series. Review nearby measurements and have the completed well tested rather than relying on a regional conclusion.
